lesson.title: Running on Autopilot: Inside the Autonomic Nervous System
lesson.summary: This section explains the autonomic nervous system, the branch of the peripheral nervous system that automatically regulates internal organs, and previews its two opposing subdivisions.
lesson.body:
Some of the body's most important work happens without any conscious effort at all. Nobody has to consciously remember to keep their heart beating, keep their lungs breathing, or keep their pupils adjusting to changing light. That automatic regulation is the job of the autonomic nervous system, one of the two subdivisions of the peripheral nervous system introduced in the previous section. Where the somatic nervous system, the other peripheral subdivision, handles voluntary movements you consciously choose to make, the autonomic nervous system handles involuntary functions of internal organs and glands that occur continuously, whether you are paying attention to them or not.

This automatic design makes a lot of sense once you think about what it frees the brain to do. If keeping your heart beating at an appropriate rate required constant conscious attention the way solving a math problem does, there would be no mental capacity left over for anything else, thinking, planning, holding a conversation, or paying attention to a genuine threat. By handing routine, life sustaining regulation over to a system that runs automatically in the background, the nervous system frees conscious awareness and effortful attention for tasks that actually benefit from them.

The autonomic nervous system itself divides into two branches that generally work in opposition to each other, functioning something like a gas pedal and a brake pedal in the same vehicle. The sympathetic branch mobilizes the body for action, increasing heart rate and preparing muscles for exertion, while the parasympathetic branch calms the body back down and supports restful functions like digestion. Each of these two branches is important enough to deserve its own full discussion, which is exactly what the next two sections provide.

A simple example shows the autonomic nervous system in action. Imagine being startled by a sudden loud noise, a car horn blaring unexpectedly close by. Your heart rate jumps, your palms may begin to sweat, and your breathing quickens, all within a second or two, and all without you ever consciously deciding that any of it should happen. That immediate, involuntary physical reaction is the autonomic nervous system doing exactly what it evolved to do, responding to a potentially important change in the environment faster than conscious, deliberate thought ever could.

Understanding the autonomic nervous system as one branch of the larger peripheral nervous system helps make sense of the whole picture built up across this section: a central nervous system that makes decisions, a peripheral nervous system that connects that decision making center to the rest of the body, a somatic branch for voluntary movement, and now an autonomic branch for involuntary regulation, which itself splits into the two opposing forces covered next.
